sources.title: Banes, Galdikas and Vigilant (2016), Reintroduction of confiscated and displaced mammals risks outbreeding and introgression in natural populations, as evidenced by orang-utans of divergent subspecies
sources.version: Scientific Reports 6, article 22026; version of record published 2016-02-25
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods, faecal sample collection and mtDNA analysis; Results, mtDNA haplotypes and parentage; Discussion
sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0), stated in the article rights notice
sources.scope: Camp Leakey, Tanjung Puting National Park, Central Kalimantan: mitochondrial DNA evidence from historical reintroduced orangutans and their descendants. The study documents one human-mediated reintroduction history and does not estimate natural range-wide gene flow. The article discloses that coauthor B.M.F.G. continued to manage Camp Leakey and a nearby rehabilitation centre.
sources.licenseAppliesTo: Article text under the item-level CC BY 4.0 notice; separately credited third-party material is excluded.
sources.attribution: Banes GL, Galdikas BMF, Vigilant L (2016). Scientific Reports 6:22026. https://doi.org/10.1038/srep22026. Claims are paraphrased.

gaps: No morphology evidence was assessed in this batch.
Reproduction, development, lifespan and other life-history traits have not been assessed.

claims.text: Using an updated mean nest-decay rate of 288.3 days, the study estimated about 202 orangutans within Danau Sentarum National Park (95% CI 75.67–541.79) and about 71 outside it (95% CI 20.76–244.63); these are local model-based estimates, not direct counts.
claims.locator: Results §4.3, population estimates and Table 2; Discussion §5
claims.placeTimeScope: Ten survey locations in and around Danau Sentarum National Park, Kapuas Hulu, West Kalimantan; transect surveys were conducted in 2010–2014, with nest-decay calibration observations spanning 2010–2011. Estimates are model-derived for the sampled landscape.
claims.lifeStatus: Free-ranging orangutans detected through nests in wild and logged forest transects; no captive or domesticated animals are included.

gaps: The estimate is local and method-dependent, has wide uncertainty, and does not constitute a species-wide population estimate or complete ecological account.

claims.text: At Camp Leakey in Tanjung Puting National Park, the study analyzed mtDNA from 10 presumed unrelated adults reintroduced during the 1970s and 1980s, plus one first-generation offspring sequence used to represent a deceased reintroduced female. Of the 11 mtDNA profiles representing founder lineages, nine clustered with the local P. p. wurmbii mtDNA clade, while two females clustered with P. p. pygmaeus mtDNA from northern West Kalimantan or Sarawak. Both females reproduced with local males; the paper documented at least 22 hybridized or introgressed descendants, of which at least 15 were considered living when published in 2016. This is a human-mediated lineage-mixing history at one site, not evidence of natural species-wide gene flow or a range-wide evolutionary pattern.
claims.textZh: 在印度尼西亚中加里曼丹丹戎普丁国家公园的 Camp Leakey 放归点，研究分析了 10 只在 20 世纪 70 至 80 年代放归、推定彼此无亲缘关系的成年个体的线粒体 DNA，并用一只第一代后代的序列代表一只已死亡的放归雌体。代表 11 条放归创始谱系的 mtDNA 序列中，9 条与当地 P. p. wurmbii 线粒体 DNA 支系聚类，另两只雌体则与西加里曼丹北部或砂捞越的 P. p. pygmaeus 聚类。两只雌体都与当地雄性繁殖；截至论文 2016 年发表时，研究记录了至少 22 个杂交或渐渗后代，其中至少 15 个被认为仍存活。这是单一地点的人为介入谱系混合史，不代表自然的全种基因流或整个分布区的演化格局。
claims.locator: Abstract; Methods, faecal sample collection and mtDNA analysis; Results, mtDNA haplotypes and parentage; Discussion
claims.placeTimeScope: Camp Leakey, Tanjung Puting National Park, Central Kalimantan, Indonesia; founder releases occurred in the 1970s and 1980s. The study analyzed 10 presumed unrelated adult reintroduced orangutans plus one offspring sequence representing a deceased reintroduced female; descendant counts are those reported in 2016.
claims.lifeStatus: Orangutans sampled through faeces from a free-ranging, historically reintroduced population and descendants; the evidence includes human-mediated translocation and is not a captive-only sample.

gaps: Evidence is limited to mitochondrial lineages and descendants from one historical reintroduction site; it does not characterize genome-wide ancestry, natural range-wide gene flow, or the evolutionary history of all populations.
The study's local survey sites do not provide a complete current or historical species range inventory.
No fossil evidence or geological age was assessed.
No formal Red List, legal status or range-wide trend assessment was assessed.

reasons: Only two targeted studies were assessed; morphology, life history, distribution, fossil and conservation facets remain not-assessed, while ecology and evolution are partial.
The evidence covers a local nest-survey landscape and one human-mediated reintroduction history, not a systematic review or complete species account.
No independent expert review has been completed.

sources.version: Landscape Ecology 31:1849–1862, version of record published online 2016-03-29; issue dated October 2016

Movement patterns of three arboreal primates in a Neotropical moist forest explained by LiDAR-estimated canopy structure. Landscape Ecology 31:1849–1862. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10980-016-0367-9. CC BY 4.0. Claims paraphrased; changes made.
sources.scope: Primary movement and LiDAR study at Barro Colorado Island, Panama. The Ateles geoffroyi analysis is limited to one subadult female tracked for six months in 2011 and LiDAR collected in September 2009; no species-wide movement estimate is claimed.

claims.text: A comparative CT study found smaller nasal-turbinate surface area in 15 Ateles geoffroyi specimens than in eight Alouatta palliata specimens (Dunn post hoc p = 0.0001); the difference persisted after adjustment for skull size. The Ateles specimens' geographic provenance, collection dates and wild/captive status were not reported, so this sample does not establish species-wide anatomical variation.
claims.locator: Methods §2(c)(i); Results §3(a)(ii), “Sensory anatomy”; Fig. 2b and Fig. S3a. The study measured CT scans from 15 A. geoffroyi, eight A. palliata and two Cebus imitator specimens.
claims.placeTimeScope: Comparative CT specimen sample identified as Ateles geoffroyi; locality, collection dates and provenance of the 15 specimens are not reported in the article.
claims.lifeStatus: Museum CT specimens; the study does not report whether the source animals were wild or captive.

gaps: Only a comparative nasal-turbinate measure is supported. Specimen provenance and life status, diagnostic morphology, age-sex variation and broader anatomical variation remain unassessed; this sample is not a species-wide survey.
Reproduction, development, lifespan and other life-history traits have not been assessed.

claims.text: At the Osa Peninsula study sites, vertebrate visits to spider-monkey sleeping-site latrines were recorded by camera traps, and the study reported associations between these sites and higher seedling abundance and dung-beetle biomass than comparison sites.
claims.locator: Abstract; Results §3.2 for camera-trap vertebrate visits; §§3.3–3.4, Fig. 6A and Discussion §4 for dung-beetle and seedling comparisons
claims.placeTimeScope: Osa Peninsula, southwestern Costa Rica; sleeping sites identified in 2017, camera trapping during 2018, and monthly seedling quadrats at focal latrines from August 2018 to April 2019. The results concern sampled sites and measured indicators.
claims.lifeStatus: Free-ranging Ateles geoffroyi and vertebrate visitors at wild forest sites; no captive or domesticated animals are included.

claims.text: Among trichromatic individuals in the comparative analysis of fruit-foraging sequences, Ateles geoffroyi had the highest fruit-sniffing rate of the three study species: A. geoffroyi, Cebus imitator and Alouatta palliata. Alouatta sampling combined Sector Santa Rosa observations with supplemental records from Isla Agaltepec; the result is limited to study samples and does not establish a species-wide rate.
claims.locator: Abstract; Methods §§2(a), 2(e)(ii); Results §3(a)(iii), Fig. 3a and Table S5; Supplementary Results S1; Discussion §4(a)(i).
claims.placeTimeScope: Focal observations include Sector Santa Rosa, Área de Conservación Guanacaste, Costa Rica, and supplemental Alouatta palliata observations from Isla Agaltepec, Mexico; continuous focal samples lasted 1–10 minutes. This comparison is limited to study samples and does not assign a species-wide frequency.
claims.lifeStatus: Wild, free-ranging Ateles geoffroyi observed while foraging; captive animals are not included.

claims.text: For one subadult female Ateles geoffroyi at Barro Colorado Island, movement-step selection was positively associated with canopy height, distance from canopy gaps using an 8-m vegetation cutoff, and crown thickness. The spider-monkey model had a mean cross-validation Spearman correlation of 0.94; this is an individual-level model result, not a species-wide estimate.
claims.locator: Methods, “Animal movement patterns”; Results, “Movement patterns and forest structure”; Table 2. GPS tracking used 15-minute fixes over six months; the retained data set contained 5,537 positions.
claims.placeTimeScope: Barro Colorado Island, Panama; one subadult female tracked for six months in 2011 from roughly sunrise to sunset; LiDAR data were collected in September 2009.
claims.lifeStatus: One free-ranging subadult female; no other age-sex classes or populations are represented by the movement track.

gaps: The studies cover selected Costa Rican sites and one tracked individual in Panama. Range-wide habitat use, seasonal and population variation, causal effects, and long-term population consequences remain unassessed.
No phylogenetic or evolutionary evidence was assessed.
A species-wide range inventory and locality history were not assessed; study-site location alone is not a range account.
No fossil evidence or geological age was assessed.
No threat status, trend or range-wide conservation assessment was assessed.

reasons: Three source-linked studies support limited morphology and field ecology; life history, evolution, distribution, fossil and conservation facets remain not-assessed.
The evidence concerns one CT sample, selected Costa Rican study sites and one tracked female in Panama; it is not a systematic review or complete species account.
No independent expert review has been completed.
